function_status: Multiple alleles: *1 normal, *4 no function, *5 deletion, *10 decreased, *41 decreased
text_chunk: CYP2D6 (Cytochrome P450 2D6) is located on chromosome 22q13.2 and is responsible for Phase I oxidative metabolism of approximately 25% of clinically used drugs including codeine, tramadol, tamoxifen, atomoxetine, ondansetron, and many antidepressants. CYP2D6 is highly polymorphic with over 150 star alleles defined. Key no-function alleles include *3 (frameshift), *4 (splicing defect, most common in Europeans), *5 (gene deletion), and *6 (frameshift). Decreased function alleles include *9, *10 (most common in East Asians), *17 (most common in Africans), *29, and *41. Gene duplications (*1xN, *2xN) cause ultra-rapid metabolism. Structural variation including deletions, duplications, tandem arrangements, and hybrids with CYP2D7 makes genotyping complex. CPIC guidelines exist for codeine, tramadol, tamoxifen, ondansetron, atomoxetine, venlafaxine, and eliglustat.

function_status: Multiple alleles: *1 normal, *2 no function, *3 no function, *17 increased function
text_chunk: CYP2C19 (Cytochrome P450 2C19) on chromosome 10q23.33 metabolizes approximately 10% of clinically used drugs including clopidogrel, PPIs, voriconazole, and several antidepressants (escitalopram, citalopram, sertraline, amitriptyline). The *2 allele (splicing defect) is the most common loss-of-function allele globally. The *3 allele (premature stop codon) is most prevalent in East Asian populations. The *17 allele confers increased function through enhanced transcription. CPIC Level A guidelines exist for clopidogrel (where poor metabolizers have markedly reduced active metabolite formation and increased cardiovascular event risk) and voriconazole. CYP2C19 genotyping is among the most clinically impactful PGx tests due to widespread clopidogrel use.

function_status: Multiple alleles: *1 normal, *2 decreased, *3 decreased, *6 no function
text_chunk: CYP2C9 (Cytochrome P450 2C9) on chromosome 10q23.33 metabolizes approximately 15% of drugs including warfarin (S-warfarin), phenytoin, NSAIDs, and sulfonylureas. The *2 (R144C) and *3 (I359L) alleles are the most common decreased-function variants, particularly in European populations. CYP2C9 genotype is a major determinant of warfarin dose requirements alongside VKORC1 and CYP4F2. Poor metabolizers (*3/*3) require approximately 80% lower warfarin maintenance doses. CPIC guidelines exist for warfarin, phenytoin, celecoxib, and several other NSAIDs.

function_status: *1 normal, *1B possible increased expression, *22 decreased function
text_chunk: CYP3A4 (Cytochrome P450 3A4) on chromosome 7q22.1 is the most abundant hepatic CYP enzyme, responsible for Phase I metabolism of approximately 30% of all clinically used drugs. Unlike CYP2D6 and CYP2C19, CYP3A4 has relatively few clinically actionable genetic variants. The *22 allele (intron 6 SNP, rs35599367) is associated with decreased expression and reduced metabolism of substrates like tacrolimus. CYP3A4 phenotype is more strongly influenced by drug-drug interactions (inhibition by azole antifungals, macrolides; induction by rifampin, carbamazepine) than by genetics. CPIC guidelines reference CYP3A4 for tacrolimus dosing.

function_status: *1 expresser (normal), *3 non-expresser (no function)
text_chunk: CYP3A5 (Cytochrome P450 3A5) on chromosome 7q22.1 is clinically relevant for tacrolimus dosing in transplant patients. The *3 allele (splice defect, rs776746) is the most common loss-of-function allele and results in non-expression of the enzyme. CYP3A5 expressers (*1/*1 or *1/*3) require higher tacrolimus doses (1.5-2x) to achieve therapeutic trough levels. The *1 allele frequency varies dramatically by ethnicity: ~70% in African populations, ~25% in East Asians, and ~6% in Europeans. CPIC provides Level A guidelines for CYP3A5-guided tacrolimus dosing.

function_status: *1 normal, *1C decreased inducibility, *1F increased inducibility, *1K decreased function
text_chunk: CYP1A2 (Cytochrome P450 1A2) on chromosome 15q24.1 metabolizes caffeine, theophylline, clozapine, and olanzapine. The *1F allele is associated with increased inducibility, meaning carriers who smoke or consume cruciferous vegetables have even higher CYP1A2 activity. Phenotype is heavily influenced by environmental factors: smoking induces CYP1A2 2-4 fold, while fluvoxamine is a potent inhibitor. No CPIC guidelines currently exist for CYP1A2, but its role in clozapine metabolism is clinically important for dose adjustment in psychiatric pharmacotherapy.

function_status: *1 normal, *4 increased function, *6 decreased function, *18 no function
text_chunk: CYP2B6 (Cytochrome P450 2B6) on chromosome 19q13.2 metabolizes efavirenz, methadone, bupropion, and cyclophosphamide. The *6 allele (Q172H + K262R) is the most common decreased-function variant, with frequencies of ~25% globally. CYP2B6 poor metabolizers have significantly elevated efavirenz plasma levels, increasing risk of CNS side effects. CPIC provides guidelines for efavirenz dosing based on CYP2B6 genotype, recommending dose reduction from 600mg to 400mg in poor metabolizers.

function_status: *1 normal function, *3 decreased vitamin K1 oxidase activity
text_chunk: CYP4F2 (Cytochrome P450 4F2) on chromosome 19p13.12 functions as a vitamin K1 oxidase. The *3 allele (V433M, rs2108622) causes decreased vitamin K metabolism, leading to higher hepatic vitamin K levels and therefore higher warfarin dose requirements (approximately 1 mg/day increase). CYP4F2 genotype is incorporated into pharmacogenomic warfarin dosing algorithms alongside CYP2C9 and VKORC1. The *3 allele frequency is approximately 30% in Europeans, 22% in East Asians, and 7% in Africans.

function_status: -1639A associated with low expression and warfarin sensitivity; D36Y and V66M cause warfarin resistance
text_chunk: VKORC1 (Vitamin K Epoxide Reductase Complex Subunit 1) on chromosome 16p11.2 is the pharmacological target of warfarin. The -1639G>A promoter SNP (rs9923231) is the strongest single genetic predictor of warfarin dose, explaining approximately 25% of dose variability. The A allele reduces VKORC1 expression, resulting in increased warfarin sensitivity and lower dose requirements. The A allele is very common in East Asians (~90%), moderately common in Europeans (~40%), and less common in Africans (~10%), contributing to the observed inter-ethnic differences in warfarin dosing. Rare missense variants (D36Y, V66M, R58G) cause warfarin resistance requiring very high doses.

function_status: *1 normal, *2A no function, *13 no function, D949V decreased function, HapB3 decreased function
text_chunk: DPYD (Dihydropyrimidine Dehydrogenase) on chromosome 1p21.3 encodes the rate-limiting enzyme for fluoropyrimidine catabolism (5-fluorouracil, capecitabine). DPYD deficiency causes severe, potentially fatal toxicity including grade 4 neutropenia, mucositis, and death. The *2A allele (IVS14+1G>A, splice site) and *13 (I560S) are no-function variants. D949V and HapB3 are decreased-function variants with activity scores of 0.5. CPIC and European guidelines mandate pre-treatment DPYD testing. The EMA requires DPYD testing before all fluoropyrimidine therapy since 2020. Partial deficiency (activity score 1.0-1.5) requires 25-50% dose reduction; complete deficiency is a contraindication.

function_status: *1 normal, *2 no function, *3A no function (*3B+*3C), *3B decreased, *3C decreased
text_chunk: TPMT (Thiopurine S-Methyltransferase) on chromosome 6p22.3 metabolizes thiopurine drugs (azathioprine, mercaptopurine, thioguanine). TPMT deficiency leads to accumulation of cytotoxic thioguanine nucleotides causing severe myelosuppression. The *3A allele (combines *3B A154T and *3C Y240C) is the most common variant in Europeans (~5%). The *3C allele alone is most common in East Asians and Africans. CPIC guidelines recommend starting azathioprine/mercaptopurine at 30-70% of standard dose for intermediate metabolizers and considering alternative agents or 10% dose with frequent monitoring for poor metabolizers. Both TPMT and NUDT15 should be tested together.

function_status: *1 normal, *2 no function, *3 no function, *4 decreased, *5 decreased
text_chunk: NUDT15 (Nudix Hydrolase 15) on chromosome 13q14.2 dephosphorylates thioguanine nucleotides. NUDT15 deficiency, like TPMT deficiency, causes severe thiopurine-induced myelosuppression. The *3 allele (R139C) is particularly prevalent in East Asian populations (~10%) and Hispanic/Latino populations (~4%), where it is a more important predictor of thiopurine toxicity than TPMT variants. CPIC recommends combined TPMT+NUDT15 testing for thiopurine dosing. Poor metabolizers (activity score 0) should avoid thiopurines or use 10% of standard dose with intensive monitoring.

text_chunk: UGT1A1 (UDP Glucuronosyltransferase 1A1) on chromosome 2q37.1 conjugates bilirubin and the active metabolite of irinotecan (SN-38). The *28 allele (TA7 repeat in promoter, rs8175347) reduces UGT1A1 expression, causing Gilbert syndrome and increased risk of irinotecan-induced severe neutropenia and diarrhea. The *28 allele is present in ~35-40% of Europeans and Africans. The *6 allele (G71R) is the predominant reduced-function allele in East Asians. CPIC and FDA labeling recommend reduced initial irinotecan doses for UGT1A1 poor metabolizers (*28/*28). The FDA label for irinotecan includes PGx information regarding UGT1A1*28 homozygosity.

function_status: *1a normal, *1b increased function, *5 decreased function, *15 (*1b+*5), *17 decreased function
text_chunk: SLCO1B1 (Solute Carrier Organic Anion Transporter 1B1) on chromosome 12p12.1 is a hepatic uptake transporter for statins, bilirubin, and methotrexate. The c.521T>C variant (rs4149056, *5) reduces transporter function, leading to elevated systemic statin exposure and increased risk of statin-induced myopathy. CPIC guidelines recommend prescribing an alternative statin or using a lower dose of simvastatin for SLCO1B1 poor function carriers. The SEARCH trial demonstrated that c.521CC homozygotes have a 16.9-fold increased risk of simvastatin-induced myopathy. The *5 allele frequency is approximately 15% in Europeans, 12% in East Asians, and 2% in Africans.

function_status: C3435T TT genotype associated with reduced P-glycoprotein expression
text_chunk: ABCB1 (ATP Binding Cassette Subfamily B Member 1, also known as MDR1/P-glycoprotein) on chromosome 7q21.12 is a major efflux transporter at the blood-brain barrier, intestine, liver, and kidney. It transports numerous drugs including digoxin, cyclosporine, tacrolimus, and many chemotherapy agents. The C3435T SNP (rs1045642) is the most studied variant, with the TT genotype associated with reduced intestinal P-gp expression and higher drug bioavailability. Clinical significance is debated due to inconsistent study results, and no CPIC guidelines currently exist for ABCB1.

function_status: Q141K causes decreased function; associated with reduced transport and increased drug exposure
text_chunk: ABCG2 (ATP Binding Cassette Subfamily G Member 2, also known as BCRP) on chromosome 4q22.1 is an efflux transporter important for rosuvastatin, sulfasalazine, methotrexate, and several tyrosine kinase inhibitors. The Q141K variant (rs2231142) causes protein misfolding and reduced transport activity. Carriers have increased rosuvastatin exposure (~2-fold for homozygotes) and increased risk of statin myopathy. The variant is common in East Asians (~30%) and less frequent in Europeans (~10%) and Africans (~1%). CPIC guidelines for statins include ABCG2 alongside SLCO1B1.

function_status: X-linked; A- (Class III), Mediterranean (Class II), Canton (Class II) cause enzyme deficiency
text_chunk: G6PD (Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase) on chromosome Xq28 is an X-linked enzyme critical for protecting red blood cells from oxidative stress. G6PD deficiency is the most common enzymopathy worldwide, affecting ~400 million people. Deficient individuals are at risk for acute hemolytic anemia when exposed to oxidant drugs (primaquine, dapsone, rasburicase, methylene blue, certain sulfonamides). WHO classifies variants from Class I (chronic hemolysis) to Class V (increased activity). The A- variant is most common in African populations (~20%), while the Mediterranean variant (S188F) is prevalent in Middle Eastern and Southern European populations. CPIC guidelines recommend testing G6PD status before prescribing rasburicase (contraindicated in deficiency) and primaquine.

function_status: *4 rapid acetylator, *5/*6/*7 slow acetylator alleles
text_chunk: NAT2 (N-Acetyltransferase 2) on chromosome 8p22 catalyzes Phase II acetylation of isoniazid, hydralazine, procainamide, sulfasalazine, and several aromatic amines. NAT2 acetylator phenotype (rapid, intermediate, slow) is determined by combinations of star alleles. Slow acetylators (two decreased/no-function alleles) have higher isoniazid exposure and increased risk of hepatotoxicity and peripheral neuropathy but may have better tuberculosis treatment efficacy. Approximately 50-60% of Europeans and Africans are slow acetylators, compared to ~10-20% of East Asians. CPIC does not yet have NAT2 guidelines, but DPWG provides isoniazid dosing recommendations.

text_chunk: CYP2A6 (Cytochrome P450 2A6) on chromosome 19q13.2 is the primary enzyme for nicotine metabolism, converting nicotine to cotinine. CYP2A6 also metabolizes tegafur, letrozole, valproic acid, and efavirenz. The *4 allele (gene deletion) is particularly common in East Asian populations (~20%), contributing to higher nicotine exposure per cigarette and altered smoking behavior. CYP2A6 genotype predicts nicotine replacement therapy response and smoking cessation outcomes. Slow metabolizers may benefit from lower nicotine replacement doses and show better response to non-nicotine cessation aids like varenicline.

function_status: Val/Val high activity, Val/Met intermediate, Met/Met low activity
text_chunk: COMT (Catechol-O-Methyltransferase) on chromosome 22q11.21 catalyzes the degradation of catecholamines (dopamine, norepinephrine, epinephrine) and catechol estrogens. The Val158Met polymorphism (rs4680) is a well-studied functional variant. The Met allele produces a thermolabile enzyme with 3-4 fold reduced activity, resulting in higher synaptic dopamine levels. COMT genotype influences pain sensitivity, opioid analgesic requirements, and potentially ADHD medication response. Met/Met individuals typically have greater pain sensitivity but may respond to lower opioid doses. The variant also affects response to levodopa in Parkinson disease and to tolcapone (COMT inhibitor).

function_status: A118G (N40D) associated with altered mu-opioid receptor binding and opioid response
text_chunk: OPRM1 (Opioid Receptor Mu 1) on chromosome 6q25.2 encodes the mu-opioid receptor, the primary target of morphine, codeine active metabolite, fentanyl, and other opioids. The A118G variant (rs1799971, N40D) is associated with altered receptor binding affinity and opioid response variability. G allele carriers may require higher morphine doses for adequate analgesia and show reduced opioid side effects (nausea, sedation). The G allele is most common in East Asians (~40%), less frequent in Europeans (~15%), and uncommon in Africans (~5%). OPRM1 variants also influence naltrexone response in alcohol use disorder treatment.

function_status: CC genotype associated with favorable response to pegylated interferon-alpha/ribavirin
text_chunk: IFNL3 (Interferon Lambda 3, formerly IL28B) on chromosome 19q13.2 encodes interferon lambda 3, important for innate antiviral immunity. The rs12979860 C/T polymorphism is the strongest host genetic predictor of hepatitis C virus (HCV) treatment response to pegylated interferon-alpha/ribavirin. CC homozygotes have ~2-3 fold higher sustained virologic response (SVR) rates compared to TT. While direct-acting antivirals (DAAs) have largely supplanted interferon-based HCV therapy, IFNL3 genotype remains relevant for treatment stratification in resource-limited settings and may influence spontaneous HCV clearance and liver fibrosis progression.

function_status: *31:01 associated with carbamazepine hypersensitivity; *33:03 with ticlopidine hepatotoxicity
text_chunk: HLA-A (Human Leukocyte Antigen A) on chromosome 6p21.3 is part of the MHC class I complex. HLA-A*31:01 is associated with carbamazepine-induced hypersensitivity reactions across all ethnicities, including maculopapular exanthema (MPE), drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS), and Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis (SJS/TEN). The risk allele is present in 2-8% of populations. CPIC guidelines recommend HLA-A*31:01 testing before carbamazepine initiation in populations where the allele is prevalent. HLA-A*33:03 is associated with ticlopidine-induced liver injury.

function_status: Multiple alleles associated with severe drug hypersensitivity reactions
text_chunk: HLA-B (Human Leukocyte Antigen B) on chromosome 6p21.3 is the most pharmacogenomically important HLA gene. HLA-B*57:01 is strongly associated with abacavir hypersensitivity syndrome (~100% negative predictive value). HLA-B*58:01 is associated with allopurinol-induced SJS/TEN. HLA-B*15:02 is associated with carbamazepine-, phenytoin-, and oxcarbazepine-induced SJS/TEN, predominantly in Southeast Asian populations. HLA-B*13:01 is linked to dapsone hypersensitivity syndrome. Pre-prescription HLA-B*57:01 testing for abacavir and HLA-B*15:02 testing for carbamazepine in at-risk populations are among the most widely implemented PGx tests globally.

function_status: Pathogenic variants predispose to malignant hyperthermia susceptibility (MHS)
text_chunk: RYR1 (Ryanodine Receptor 1) on chromosome 19q13.2 encodes the skeletal muscle calcium release channel. Pathogenic variants in RYR1 (and less commonly CACNA1S) cause Malignant Hyperthermia Susceptibility (MHS), a pharmacogenetic condition triggered by volatile anesthetic agents (sevoflurane, desflurane, isoflurane) and succinylcholine. MHS is a life-threatening hypermetabolic crisis with mortality exceeding 70% if untreated. Dantrolene is the specific treatment. Over 400 RYR1 variants have been identified, but only ~40 are classified as pathogenic/diagnostic. Family history of MH events or unexplained perioperative death should prompt genetic testing. CPIC provides Level A guidelines for volatile anesthetics and succinylcholine based on RYR1/CACNA1S genotype.
